analysis.one_liner: Makes wealthy universities pay a share of student costs and share loan default losses.
analysis.headline: A bill requiring universities with billion-dollar endowments to cover up to 75% of enrolled students' costs never got a committee vote and died at the end of the 118th Congress.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require any college receiving federal aid that holds an endowment over $1 billion to pay part of each full-time student's cost of attendance: 25% for endowments over $1 billion, 50% over $5 billion, and 75% over $10 billion. It would also make colleges repay the Education Department a rising share, eventually 25%, of the loan balances of their former students who default, and would require colleges to publish graduation, employment, wage, and debt numbers for every degree program.
analysis.who_benefits: Full-time students at colleges with large endowments, who would see a large share of their cost of attendance covered by the school instead of paid through tuition and loans. Students and families everywhere would gain from public data on how much each degree program costs and what its graduates earn and owe. Taxpayers gain indirectly if colleges, facing default penalties, steer students toward programs that actually lead to repayment.

how_it_helps.text: Colleges with endowments over $1 billion must pay a set share of each full-time student's cost of attendance: 25% for endowments of $1–5 billion, 50% for $5–10 billion, and 75% for $10 billion or more.

Colleges must send the Education Department an escalating 'risk-sharing' payment each year, starting at 1% and reaching 25% by year 25, of the loan balance of students who entered repayment and later defaulted, giving schools a financial stake in whether their graduates can repay.
Colleges must report, and the department must publish, program-by-program data including graduation rates, employment, graduates' median wages, total cost of each degree, and average student debt.
Schools must file an annual report on their endowment size and growth, explaining any increase in cost of attendance.

analysis.who_pays: Colleges and universities with endowments above $1 billion, which would draw on endowment income or other funds to cover student costs and would owe payments when their graduates default. The bill applies the endowment mandate to every institution over the threshold, including smaller private colleges with $1 billion endowments, not only the wealthiest research universities.

drawbacks.text: The default risk-sharing penalty gives colleges a financial reason to admit fewer low-income and first-generation students, who are statistically more likely to default, unless the bill's structure prevents that; this text contains no such safeguard.

The cost-match mandate covers any institution with an endowment over $1 billion, including small private colleges whose endowments are largely restricted by donors to specific purposes, which could strain schools that are not wealthy in the way the bill assumes.

The bill shifts costs from students to college endowments but does nothing about tuition levels themselves; colleges could raise sticker prices to offset the required contributions, and the annual cost-of-attendance report requires only an explanation of increases, not a limit on them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea, that institutions sitting on billion-dollar endowments should bear more of their students' costs and share the loss when their graduates default, directly shifts money from concentrated wealth to students. The honest concerns are real: default penalties can push schools away from the very students most likely to need help, and a $1 billion threshold sweeps in colleges that are not wealthy by elite-university standards. The transparency requirements are uncontroversial and cheap. On balance the bill targets a concentrated interest without clearly harming students, but it needed the safeguards its drafters did not include.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate's education committee, where it sat without a hearing, amendment, or vote until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Rick Scott introduced the bill on November 29, 2023, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
No other senator cosponsored the bill; the cosponsor list shows zero, with no support from either party.
The committee took no further action, and the bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Colleges with billion-dollar endowments keep those funds untouched, owe nothing when their graduates default, and face no new disclosure of program-level costs and outcomes. Students continue to pay full tuition and bear default risk alone.

for.name: Sen. Rick Scott
for.role: U.S. Senator from Florida; bill's sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate education committee

against.name: Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions
against.role: Senate committee with jurisdiction over higher education law
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no action — no hearing, markup, or vote — for the life of the Congress

sides.party_line_note: A single Republican introduced the bill and not one senator from either party signed on, so the failure to advance was not a partisan bloc vote but an absence of any support at all.

industries.industry: Colleges and universities with billion-dollar endowments
industries.note: The bill would force these institutions to draw on endowment wealth to cover student costs and to pay when their graduates default. Their interest in blocking it runs against students', who would otherwise see a large share of tuition covered and gain real data on program value.

All aid-participating colleges would face new reporting duties on graduation, wages, and debt per program, plus endowment disclosure from large institutions. Smaller schools with endowments just over the threshold would bear costs alongside the wealthiest universities.
